questions.questionText:
On 31 December 2025, T. Nyoni's Cash Book (bank column) showed a debit balance of $2,450, whereas the Bank Statement showed $2,890.
The following differences were found:
(i) Bank charges of $45 appeared on the Bank Statement only.
(ii) A credit transfer of $310 from debtor R. Dube was received directly by the bank.
(iii) Unpresented cheques totalled $640.
(iv) Cash banked on 31 December of $465 had not yet been credited by the bank.
Prepare (a) an Updated Cash Book [4 marks] and (b) a Bank Reconciliation Statement as at 31 December 2025 [4 marks].
questions.explanation:
**(a) Updated Cash Book (Bank Column) [4 marks]:** Begin with the unadjusted Cash Book debit balance of **$2,450**. Next, scan the discrepancies to identify items that already passed through the bank account but have not yet been entered in the firm’s books: record the direct customer credit transfer from **R. Dube (+$310)** on the debit (receipts) side, and enter **Bank charges ($45)** on the credit (payments) side. Computing the adjusted balance gives **$2,450 + $310 - $45 = $2,715 (Dr)** brought down as the true cash book balance at 31 December 2025.

**(b) Bank Reconciliation Statement as at 31 December 2025 [4 marks]:** Starting cleanly from the **Adjusted Cash Book Debit balance ($2,715)**, reconcile for timing differences created by items recorded by the trader but not yet cleared at the bank. **Add Unpresented Cheques (+$640)**—cheques written to suppliers that have reduced the Cash Book yet have not left the bank—giving an intermediate subtotal of **$3,355**. **Deduct Uncredited Lodgements (-$465)** banked on 31 December that await clearing, arriving precisely at **$3,355 - $465 = $2,890 (Cr balance per Bank Statement)**.

**ZIMSEC Paper 2 Examiner Note:** Keep items strictly in their correct document: direct bank charges, dishonoured cheques, standing orders, and bank credit transfers belong inside the **Updated Cash Book** because the trader’s ledger lacked them, whereas **unpresented cheques** and **uncredited bankings** appear exclusively inside the **Bank Reconciliation Statement** because the Cash Book already reflects them accurately.

questions.questionText:
Enter the following Trial Balance adjustments for M. Chigumba for the year ended 31 December 2025 and show the exact Income Statement & Balance Sheet extracts:
- Trial balance Electricity expense: $1,800; Electricity owing at 31 Dec: $240.
- Trial balance Insurance expense: $960 (covers 12 months ending 31 March 2026).
- Delivery van cost $16,000, accumulated depreciation $3,200; depreciate at 20% reducing balance. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Year-End Accrual, Prepayment & Depreciation Computations [6 marks]:** First, for **Electricity**, unpaid December charges of **$240** must be matched into the 2025 accounting period, making the full **Income Statement charge $1,800 + $240 = $2,040** and recording **$240 as an Accrual (Other Payables) under Current Liabilities** on the Statement of Financial Position [2 marks]. Second, the **$960 Insurance payment** covers 12 months ending 31 March 2026, so **3 months (January–March 2026)** belong to the next accounting year: **Prepaid Insurance = (3 / 12) × $960 = $240** under **Current Assets (Other Receivables)**, leaving the **2025 Income Statement Insurance Expense at $960 - $240 = $720** [2 marks].

**Reducing Balance Delivery Van Depreciation:** Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is calculated on **Net Book Value (Cost minus Accumulated Depreciation)** rather than original cost. Subtracting prior accumulated depreciation gives opening Net Book Value **$16,000 - $3,200 = $12,800**; multiplying by **20%** gives the **2025 Depreciation Expense = 0.20 × $12,800 = $2,560** in the Income Statement. On the Statement of Financial Position at 31 December 2025, total **Accumulated Depreciation rises to $3,200 + $2,560 = $5,760**, leaving **Net Book Value = $16,000 - $5,760 = $10,240** [2 marks].

**Underlying Principle & Exam Precision:** Notice how all three adjustments honour the **Accruals (Matching) Concept**—expenses must reflect resources consumed during the 12-month period regardless of cash dates, while the asset base shrinks smoothly across productive use. Always double-check whether a question specifies **straight-line** (percentage of original cost) versus **reducing balance** (percentage of remaining net book value), as confusing those two methods costs straightforward marks.

questions.questionText:
From the following details of Chipo Traders, prepare the Trading and Profit & Loss Account (Income Statement) for the year ended 31 December 2025:
Sales $94,000; Sales Returns $2,000; Opening Inventory $8,500; Purchases $56,000; Carriage Inwards $1,500; Closing Inventory $10,000; Rent & Rates $7,200; Wages $11,800; Discount Received $900; General Expenses $3,400. [8 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Trading Account Section — Net Sales & Gross Profit [4 marks]:** Start at **Sales ($94,000)** and deduct **Sales Returns / Returns Inwards ($2,000)** to obtain **Net Turnover = $92,000** [1 mark]. Next compute **Cost of Goods Sold (Cost of Sales)**: begin with **Opening Inventory ($8,500)**, add **Purchases ($56,000)** and **Carriage Inwards ($1,500)**—because freight incurred bringing stock into the warehouse is part of inventory acquisition cost—totalling **$66,000 Cost of Goods Available for Sale**, then subtract **Closing Inventory ($10,000)** to reach **Cost of Sales = $56,000** [2 marks]. Subtracting Cost of Sales from Net Sales yields **Gross Profit = $92,000 - $56,000 = $36,000** [1 mark].

**Profit & Loss Section — Other Income, Expenses & Net Profit [4 marks]:** Add **Discount Received ($900)** to Gross Profit because cash discounts earned from suppliers for prompt payment represent extra business income, raising **Total Income to $36,000 + $900 = $36,900** [1 mark]. Group all operating expenses carefully (**Rent & Rates $7,200 + Wages $11,800 + General Expenses $3,400 = $22,400**) [2 marks], then deduct total expenses from total income to calculate **Net Profit (Profit for the Year) = $36,900 - $22,400 = $14,500** [1 mark].

**Classic ZIMSEC Trading Trap to Avoid:** Never mix **Carriage Inwards** with operating expenses below Gross Profit, and never place **Discount Received** inside Expenses or Trading Account Purchases—it sits strictly right below Gross Profit as Other Operating Income. Also verify **Opening Inventory + Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Closing Inventory** using neat vertical alignment so examiners can award method marks even if one arithmetic step slips.

questions.questionText:
Prepare a Sales Ledger Control Account for August 2025 from these totals:
1 Aug Debtors balance $4,200; Credit sales $18,600; Cash received from debtors $16,400; Sales returns $520; Discount allowed $380; Bad debts written off $250; Dishonoured customer cheque $300. Find the closing Trade Receivables balance at 31 August. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Debit Entries (Items Increasing Amounts Owed by Debtors) [3 marks]:** A **Sales Ledger Control Account** summarises all individual credit customer balances inside a single Trade Receivables control ledger. Because Trade Receivables represent an **Asset**, increases appear on the **Debit side**: enter **1 Aug Balance b/d ($4,200)**, add **Credit Sales ($18,600)** made during August, and add **Dishonoured Customer Cheque ($300)** because when a customer’s cheque bounces at the bank, their original debt springs back alive. Total debits equal **$4,200 + $18,600 + $300 = $23,100**.

**Credit Entries & Closing Trade Receivables Balance [3 marks]:** Items reducing total debts owed by credit customers go on the **Credit side**: **Cash received from debtors ($16,400)**, **Sales Returns ($520)**, **Discount Allowed ($380)** granted for timely settlement, and **Bad Debts written off ($250)**—totalling **$16,400 + $520 + $380 + $250 = $17,550** [2 marks]. Subtracting total credits from total debits gives the **31 August Closing Balance c/d = $23,100 - $17,550 = $5,550 (Dr balance brought down on 1 September)** [1 mark].

**Exam Rules & Excluded Items:** Always check every item given in Control Account problems for distractors such as **Cash Sales** or **Provision for Doubtful Debts**—neither belongs in the Sales Ledger Control Account because Cash Sales never create credit debtors and Provision for Doubtful Debts sits in its own separate ledger account. Remember that a bounced (**dishonoured**) cheque ALWAYS debits Trade Receivables back up because cash never actually cleared!

questions.questionText:
Show journal entries (with brief narratives) to correct the following errors after a Trial Balance had a Suspense credit balance of $540:
(a) Credit sales of $800 to P. Gumbo were completely omitted from the books.
(b) Repairs to office computer of $270 were debited in error to the Office Equipment account.
(c) The Purchases Day Book was overcast (added up too high) by $540. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Journal Entries (a) Error of Omission & (b) Error of Principle [4 marks]:** To correct **(a)** where an $800 credit sale to customer **P. Gumbo** was never entered anywhere, simply post the omitted double entry: **Debit P. Gumbo (Trade Receivables) $800; Credit Sales $800** *(Narrative: Correction of omitted credit sale to P. Gumbo)* [2 marks]. For **(b)** where $270 spent on recurring repairs was capitalised into **Office Equipment** (**Error of Principle** violating capital vs revenue classification), remove it from the asset account and charge the proper expense: **Debit Computer Repairs $270; Credit Office Equipment $270** *(Narrative: Correction of error of principle misclassifying repairs as equipment)* [2 marks].

**Journal Entry (c) Purchases Day Book Overcast & Suspense Elimination [2 marks]:** Because the Purchases Day Book total was added up **$540 too high**, excessive debits of $540 entered the **Purchases Account**, throwing Trial Balance totals out and leaving a temporary **$540 Credit balance inside the Suspense Account** to force balance. To cancel both faults cleanly, **Debit Suspense $540; Credit Purchases $540** *(Narrative: Correction of overcast Purchases Day Book reducing Purchases and clearing Suspense balance)*—dropping the Suspense Account precisely to **$0**!

**Distinguishing Errors Affecting vs Not Affecting Trial Balance Totals:** Notice that errors **(a)** and **(b)** never touch the **Suspense Account** because equal debits and credits were omitted or posted into the wrong class of account—Trial Balance column totals still balanced identically! Only single-sided casting errors like **(c)** disturb Trial Balance equality and require an entry against **Suspense**. Always include clear **dates/labels and one-line narratives** under every General Journal entry for full ZIMSEC presentation credit.

questions.questionText:
Kudzai and Farai are in partnership sharing profits and losses 3 : 2. Net Profit before appropriation is $42,000. Capital balances: Kudzai $40,000, Farai $30,000. Interest on capital is 10% p.a. Farai receives an annual partnership salary of $8,000. Interest on drawings: Kudzai $600, Farai $400.
Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account for the year. [7 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Step 1 — Starting Profit & Interest on Drawings [2 marks]:** Prepare the **Partnership Profit and Loss Appropriation Account** starting with **Net Profit ($42,000)** brought down from the Profit & Loss Account. Add **Interest on Drawings** charged to partners to discourage excessive personal withdrawals: **Kudzai ($600) + Farai ($400) = $1,000**, raising total **Appropriable Profit Available for Distribution to $42,000 + $1,000 = $43,000**.

**Step 2 — Interest on Capital, Partner Salary & Residual Profit Split [5 marks]:** Next deduct prior partnership entitlements per the partnership agreement before sharing the remainder. Compute **10% Interest on Capital**: **Kudzai = 10% × $40,000 = $4,000**, **Farai = 10% × $30,000 = $3,000**, totalling **$7,000** [2 marks]; then deduct **Farai’s Partnership Salary ($8,000)** [1 mark]. Subtracting **$7,000 + $8,000 = $15,000** leaves **Residual Profit = $43,000 - $15,000 = $28,000** [1 mark], divided **3 : 2 (five equal parts of $5,600)**: **Kudzai receives (3/5) × $28,000 = $16,800**, and **Farai receives (2/5) × $28,000 = $11,200** [2 marks].

**Ledger Connection & Paper 2 Discipline:** Verify your arithmetic immediately (**$16,800 + $11,200 = $28,000; + $15,000 = $43,000**) and remember that partner **Salaries, Interest on Capital, and Profit Shares** are credited inside each partner’s **Current Account**, whereas **Drawings and Interest on Drawings** are debited there. Never confuse a **Partnership Salary** with employee wages—employee wages reduce Net Profit *inside* Profit & Loss, whereas partner salaries distribute profit *inside* Appropriation.

questions.questionText:
A manufacturing firm reports for the year:
Opening raw materials $6,000; Raw material purchases $38,000; Closing raw materials $7,500; Direct factory wages $24,000; Factory power & rent $9,500; Depreciation of factory plant $4,000; Opening Work-in-Progress $3,200; Closing Work-in-Progress $2,700.
Calculate (a) Cost of Raw Materials Consumed, (b) Prime Cost, and (c) Total Production Cost of finished goods. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Raw Materials Consumed & (b) Prime Cost [4 marks]:** First calculate **Cost of Raw Materials Consumed**: add **Opening Raw Materials Inventory ($6,000)** plus **Raw Material Purchases ($38,000)** giving **$44,000** available, then deduct **Closing Raw Materials Inventory ($7,500)** to obtain **Raw Materials Consumed = $36,500** [2 marks]. Second, add **Direct Factory Wages ($24,000)**—all direct production labour traceable directly to finished output—yielding **Prime Cost = $36,500 + $24,000 = $60,500** [2 marks].

**(c) Factory Overheads, Work-in-Progress & Total Production Cost [2 marks]:** Add indirect factory running costs (**Factory Power & Rent $9,500 + Depreciation of Factory Plant $4,000 = $13,500 Factory Overheads**) onto Prime Cost to give **Gross Factory Cost = $60,500 + $13,500 = $74,000**. Finally adjust for partly finished goods (**Add Opening Work-in-Progress +$3,200; Deduct Closing Work-in-Progress -$2,700**, a net **+$500** adjustment), yielding **Total Production Cost of Finished Goods = $74,000 + $3,200 - $2,700 = $74,500**.

**Key Manufacturing Account Rules for 4051/02:** Never add office administration, delivery van costs, or sales showroom expenses inside a Manufacturing Account—only direct materials, direct factory wages/royalties, and **factory** overheads belong there! Note that **Production Cost of Finished Goods ($74,500)** transfers cleanly across to replace normal **Purchases** inside the firm’s **Trading Account**, allowing wholesalers’ margins and finished-goods Gross Profit to be measured accurately.

questions.questionText:
Mbare Sports Club had 120 members each paying $50 annual subscription. On 1 Jan 2025, 4 members owed subscriptions for 2024 and 6 members had paid for 2025 in advance. During 2025, cash received for subscriptions totalled $5,900. On 31 Dec 2025, 5 members had prepaid for 2026.
Prepare the Subscriptions Account showing the income transferred to Income & Expenditure Account and closing arrears. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Opening Balances & Cash Received inside Subscriptions Account [2 marks]:** Because a **Subscriptions Account** combines debtor and creditor balances simultaneously for a non-profit club, keep debit and credit meanings crystal clear: **Debit side opening balance** represents **Subscriptions in Arrears ($200 = 4 × $50)** owed *by* members from 2024, while **Credit side opening balance** represents **Subscriptions in Advance ($300 = 6 × $50)** prepaid for 2025 [1 mark]. When **$5,900 cash is received** during 2025 (**Debit Bank $5,900**), **Credit Subscriptions Account $5,900** [1 mark].

**Transferring True Annual Income & Calculating Closing Arrears [4 marks]:** Total **2025 Subscription Income** earned by Mbare Sports Club for all 120 members equals **120 × $50 = $6,000**—this is debited inside Subscriptions Account and transferred cleanly (**Credit Income & Expenditure Account $6,000**) [2 marks]. Closing **Subscriptions Prepaid for 2026** (**5 members × $50 = $250**) sits on the debit side as a closing liability balance c/d ($250 credit balance b/d for 2026). Balancing debits (**$200 + $6,000 + $250 = $6,450**) minus credits (**$300 + $5,900 = $6,200**) reveals **Closing Subscriptions in Arrears = $6,450 - $6,200 = $250 (5 unpaid members for 2025)** carried forward as a **Current Asset**!

**Balance Sheet Placement & Concept Check:** Check carefully how **Closing Arrears ($250)** represent money owed *to* the club (**Current Asset**), whereas **Closing Prepayments ($250)** represent cash received before service delivery (**Current Liability**). Using the full-year membership total (**120 × $50 = $6,000**) as the Balancing check verifies mathematically that receipts (**$5,900**) + prior advance (**$300**) - closing advance (**$250**) + closing arrears (**$250**) - opening arrears (**$200**) equals exact **$6,000** earned income!

questions.questionText:
Given for Zvikomborero Enterprises:
Sales $120,000; Cost of Goods Sold $78,000; Operating Expenses $24,000; Opening Inventory $11,000; Closing Inventory $15,000; Capital Employed $90,000.
Calculate:
(a) Gross Profit Margin (%) [2 marks]
(b) Net Profit Margin (%) [2 marks]
(c) Rate of Inventory Turnover (times) [2 marks]
(d) Return on Capital Employed (ROCE %) [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Gross Profit Margin & (b) Net Profit Margin [4 marks]:** First compute **Gross Profit = Sales ($120,000) - Cost of Goods Sold ($78,000) = $42,000**, giving **Gross Profit Margin = ($42,000 ÷ $120,000) × 100% = 35%** [2 marks]—meaning the firm keeps 35 cents gross profit from every dollar sold before overheads. Next deduct **Operating Expenses ($24,000)** to find **Net Profit = $42,000 - $24,000 = $18,000**, giving **Net Profit Margin = ($18,000 ÷ $120,000) × 100% = 15%** [2 marks]—meaning overheads absorbed 20% of revenue while 15% remained net profit.

**(c) Rate of Inventory Turnover & (d) ROCE [4 marks]:** Compute **Average Inventory = (Opening $11,000 + Closing $15,000) ÷ 2 = $13,000**, then divide **Cost of Goods Sold** by Average Inventory: **Rate of Inventory Turnover = $78,000 ÷ $13,000 = 6 times** per year (equivalently once roughly every 61 days!) [2 marks]. For **Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)**, divide **Net Profit** by **Capital Employed**: **ROCE = ($18,000 ÷ $90,000) × 100% = 20%** [2 marks], confirming owners earn a healthy 20 cents per dollar invested compared against standard bank deposit interest.

**Examiner Precision on Ratios & Units:** Notice three strict Paper 2 ratio rules: **(1) Inventory Turnover uses COST OF GOODS SOLD** (never Sales!), and is expressed cleanly in **times** (not percentages or dollars); **(2) Profit Margins use Net Turnover (Sales)** in the denominator and are written with **%**; and **(3) ROCE measures overall profitability against long-term Capital Employed**, serving as the primary yardstick of management efficiency.

questions.questionText:
A machine was bought on 1 Jan 2023 for $18,000 cash. Depreciation is charged at 25% per annum straight-line with nil residual value. On 30 June 2025, the machine was sold for $7,200 by cheque (assume full year depreciation in year of purchase, none in year of sale).
Prepare the Machine Disposal Account showing profit or loss on sale. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Accumulated Depreciation Calculation (Straight-Line) [2 marks]:** Under the business policy (**25% per annum straight-line, full year in purchase year, none in year of sale**), annual depreciation equals **25% × Original Cost ($18,000) = $4,500 per year**. Charging a full year in **2023 ($4,500)** and a full year in **2024 ($4,500)**—with zero charged in 2025 because the machine was sold mid-year on 30 June—produces **Total Accumulated Depreciation at disposal = $4,500 + $4,500 = $9,000** (leaving **Net Book Value = $18,000 - $9,000 = $9,000**).

**Machine Disposal Account Entries & Loss on Sale [3 marks]:** Open the **Machine Disposal Account** with three core transfers: **(1) Debit Disposal Account $18,000** (*Credit Machinery Cost Account* to remove original asset cost); **(2) Credit Disposal Account $9,000** (*Debit Provision for Depreciation* to clear accumulated depreciation); and **(3) Credit Disposal Account $7,200** (*Debit Bank* to record sale cheque proceeds) [2 marks]. Comparing total debits (**$18,000**) against total credits (**$9,000 + $7,200 = $16,200**) shows a credit balancing shortfall of **$1,800 Loss on Disposal** (*Debit Profit & Loss Account $1,800; Credit Disposal $1,800*), matching exact **Net Book Value ($9,000) - Sale Proceeds ($7,200) = $1,800 loss** [1 mark].

**Exam Verification & Depreciation Policy Warning:** Always read disposal questions word-for-word for whether depreciation is charged **pro-rata by months** (which would add 6 months’ depreciation in 2025!) or **full year in purchase / nil in disposal** as stated here—missing that single clause flips accumulated depreciation and profit/loss completely. Whenever **Proceeds ($7,200) < Net Book Value ($9,000)**, the firm sold the asset below carrying value and suffered a **Loss on Sale**.

questions.questionText:
A trader did not keep full double-entry records. At 1 Jan 2025: Cash $1,200, Equipment $8,000, Inventory $4,500, Trade Receivables $2,800, Trade Payables $2,500. During the year she drew $3,600 for personal use and banked $2,000 extra capital. At 31 Dec 2025: Cash $1,900, Equipment $7,200, Inventory $5,200, Trade Receivables $3,400, Trade Payables $2,100.
Calculate (a) Opening Capital, (b) Closing Capital, and (c) Net Profit for 2025. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Opening & (b) Closing Capital via Statements of Affairs [4 marks]:** Without complete double-entry ledgers, capital at any date is calculated using the **Accounting Equation (Capital = Total Assets - Total Liabilities)**: at **1 Jan 2025**, sum Opening Assets (**Cash $1,200 + Equipment $8,000 + Inventory $4,500 + Trade Receivables $2,800 = $16,500**) and subtract Trade Payables (**$2,500**) to get **Opening Capital = $14,000** [2 marks]. At **31 Dec 2025**, sum Closing Assets (**Cash $1,900 + Equipment $7,200 + Inventory $5,200 + Trade Receivables $3,400 = $17,700**) and subtract Closing Trade Payables (**$2,100**) to get **Closing Capital = $15,600** [2 marks].

**(c) Calculating Net Profit from Capital Growth [2 marks]:** Use the single-entry Net Profit formula **Net Profit = Closing Capital + Drawings - Additional Capital Introduced - Opening Capital**. Adding back **Drawings ($3,600)**—because personal withdrawals shrank closing equity—and deducting **Extra Capital Introduced ($2,000)**—which boosted equity without trading—gives **Net Profit = $15,600 + $3,600 - $2,000 - $14,000 = $3,200**.

**Why Drawings Are Added Back & Extra Capital Subtracted:** Think cleanly using logical proof: Opening Capital (**$14,000**) + Extra Cash Injected (**$2,000**) = **$16,000** funds invested; minus **$3,600** spent personally leaves **$12,400**—yet the business actually holds **$15,600** at year-end, proving trading generated **$3,200 Net Profit**! Notice also how Equipment declined from **$8,000 to $7,200**, naturally capturing $800 implicit depreciation directly inside Closing Capital.

questions.questionText: State the difference between Bad Debts and Provision for Doubtful Debts, and show the Ledger entries when a customer owes $900, $400 is written off as irrecoverable, and a 5% provision is created on the remaining receivables balance of $10,000. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Distinction Between Bad Debts and Provision for Doubtful Debts [2 marks]:** **Bad Debts** are confirmed **irrecoverable accounts** where specific customers are bankrupt, deceased, or untraceable, so the debt is written off permanently as an immediate expense (**Dr Bad Debts, Cr Customer Account**). By contrast, a **Provision for Doubtful Debts** is a **prudent estimated allowance** set aside at year-end against *existing* debtors who have not yet defaulted but statistically may fail to pay later—keeping the specific customer’s personal ledger open while reducing Net Trade Receivables on the Statement of Financial Position.

**Exact Double-Entry Ledger Postings [3 marks]:** For the customer owing $900 where **$400 is written off irrecoverably** (leaving $500 presumably disputed/recoverable inside the remaining $10,000 receivables), post **Debit Bad Debts Account $400; Credit Customer Account $400** (then transfer **$400 to Debit Profit & Loss Account** at year-end). Next compute the new **5% Provision** on the remaining **$10,000** receivables balance: **5% × $10,000 = $500**. Since no previous provision existed, create it by **Debiting Profit & Loss Account $500; Crediting Provision for Doubtful Debts Account $500**.

**Statement Presentation & Prudence Concept:** On the **Statement of Financial Position**, present **Trade Receivables ($10,000) less Provision for Doubtful Debts ($500) = Net Realisable Trade Receivables ($9,500)**, upholding both the **Prudence Concept** (never overstating assets) and the **Accruals Concept** (matching credit-sale losses into the year those sales occurred). Notice why Bad Debts ($400) reduce the customer’s personal balance directly whereas Provision ($500) sits in a separate **Provision account** without wiping individual customer bills.

questions.questionText: List six steps in the accounting cycle in logical chronological order from source documents to final financial statements. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Steps 1 to 3 — Source Documents, Books of Prime Entry & Ledger Posting [3 marks]:** First, **(1) Verify Source Documents** (sales invoices, purchase invoices, receipts, credit notes, bank deposit slips) as objective audit evidence of every transaction [1 mark]. Second, **(2) Journalise in Books of Prime Entry**—grouping credit sales in the Sales Journal, credit purchases in the Purchases Journal, returns in Returns Journals, cash/bank flows in the Cash Book, and unusual adjustments in the General Journal [1 mark]. Third, **(3) Post Double-Entry Ledger Accounts**, transferring individual customer/supplier lines into Sales/Purchases Ledgers and totals into the General Ledger ensuring every debit equals a credit [1 mark].

**Steps 4 to 6 — Trial Balance, Adjustments & Financial Statements [3 marks]:** Fourth, **(4) Balance Ledger Accounts & Extract a Trial Balance** to confirm total debits equal total credits mathematically [1 mark]. Fifth, **(5) Record Year-End Adjustments** (closing inventory, accruals, prepayments, depreciation, bad/doubtful debts) via General Journal entries [1 mark]. Sixth, **(6) Prepare Financial Statements**—compiling the **Income Statement** (to measure Gross and Net Profit) and **Statement of Financial Position** (reporting Assets, Liabilities, and Owner’s Equity at period-end), then closing nominal revenue/expense accounts cleanly for the new year [1 mark].

**Why Systematic Order Prevents Accounting Fraud & Errors:** Skipping source documents breaks audit verification under **Objectivity**, while skipping Books of Prime Entry would bury the General Ledger under thousands of tiny daily receipts. Notice also that even when Step 4’s **Trial Balance agrees**, hidden **Errors of Omission, Commission, Principle, or Reversal** can still linger—making careful control reconciliations and Step 5 reviews indispensable before Step 6 statements are signed off.

questions.questionText: Distinguish between a Two-Column Cash Book and a Three-Column Cash Book, and explain why the Discount columns are NOT part of double-entry cash balances. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Structural Differences Between Two-Column and Three-Column Cash Books [2 marks]:** A **Two-Column Cash Book** contains two money columns on each side (**Cash** and **Bank** on the Debit receipts side, and **Cash** and **Bank** on the Credit payments side), serving simultaneously as a journal and a ledger account for both Cash and Bank balances. A **Three-Column Cash Book** adds one extra memorandum column onto each side—**Discount Allowed (on the Debit side beside customer receipts)** and **Discount Received (on the Credit side beside supplier payments)**—so cash discounts settled on invoices sit neatly beside exact cheque/cash payments.

**Why Discount Columns Are Memorandum Only (Not Double-Entry Cash Balances) [2 marks]:** Neither **Discount Allowed** nor **Discount Received** tracks actual physical cash notes or bank funds flowing in or out; rather, they record **non-cash reductions** negotiated off customer or supplier debts for prompt settlement. Therefore, unlike Cash and Bank columns—which are balanced off with **Balance c/d / b/d**—the **Discount Allowed** and **Discount Received** columns are simply **totalled cleanly at month-end** and posted to separate General Ledger nominal accounts (**Debit Discount Allowed Account** and **Credit Discount Received Account**).

**Exam Posting Rule to Memorise:** Notice the clever directional rule in a Three-Column Cash Book: individual customer discounts entered on the **Debit side** *credit* the individual debtor’s account alongside cash paid, while their monthly column total is **Debited** to the **Discount Allowed** expense account—preserving complete debit-equals-credit symmetry without ever mixing discounts into physical bank balances!

questions.questionText: A business starts the year with $400 Provision for Doubtful Debts. Trade receivables at year-end are $14,000 and the business decides to maintain the provision at 2.5%. Calculate the adjustment to the Income Statement and state whether it is added as income or deducted as an expense. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Computing the Closing Provision & Adjustment [3 marks]:** Begin by finding the **Required Closing Provision for Doubtful Debts**: **2.5% × Closing Trade Receivables ($14,000) = 0.025 × $14,000 = $350** [2 marks]. Compare this required balance against the **Opening Provision ($400)** brought forward from last year: **$400 (Opening) - $350 (Required) = $50 Decrease in Provision** [1 mark].

**Income Statement Treatment (Added as Income) [1 mark]:** Because the business overestimated bad debt risk slightly last year ($400 was set aside, yet only $350 is needed now), **$50 of previously expensed provision is released back**. In the **Income Statement**, this **$50 decrease in Provision for Doubtful Debts is ADDED to Gross Profit** under Other Income (*never deducted as an expense!*). On the **Provision for Doubtful Debts Ledger Account**, you **Debit Provision $50** and **Credit Income Statement (P&L) $50**, leaving the updated **$350 Cr Balance c/d**.

**Quick Rule of Thumb for Provision Adjustments:** Always compare Opening versus Closing provision carefully: an **INCREASE** in Provision (**Closing > Opening**) is an **Expense** deducted from Gross Profit, whereas a **DECREASE** (**Closing < Opening**) is **Income Added** to Gross Profit! Remember to show **Net Trade Receivables = $14,000 - $350 = $13,650** on the Statement of Financial Position, NEVER subtracting the $400 old balance or $50 change!

questions.questionText: Explain the accounting treatment of (a) Carriage Inwards, (b) Carriage Outwards, (c) Drawings in cash, and (d) Owner introducing a personal computer into the business. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Carriage Inwards & (b) Carriage Outwards [2 marks]:** **Carriage Inwards** (delivery freight paid by the buyer to transport purchased inventory into the business premises) increases the true cost of acquiring stock, so it is **added to Purchases inside the Trading Account** before calculating Cost of Goods Sold and Gross Profit [1 mark]. Conversely, **Carriage Outwards** (delivery transport paid by the seller to dispatch sold goods to customers) is a selling and distribution cost, so it is charged cleanly as an **Operating Expense in the Profit & Loss Section** after Gross Profit [1 mark].

**(c) Cash Drawings & (d) Capital Introduced as Equipment [2 marks]:** **(c) Cash Drawings** represent personal withdrawals by the owner for private household use, NEVER a business operating expense—post **Debit Drawings, Credit Cash**, and **deduct Drawings from Owner’s Capital** on the Statement of Financial Position [1 mark]. **(d) Personal Computer Introduced** is additional **Capital** invested in kind rather than an expense—post **Debit Office Equipment (Non-Current Asset), Credit Capital Account**, raising both Non-Current Assets and Owner’s Equity identically [1 mark].

**Business Entity Concept Link:** Notice that **(c)** and **(d)** directly uphold the **Business Entity Concept**: the enterprise and its owner are strictly separate accounting entities! Consequently, personal drawings reduce equity without distorting net trading profit, while an owner contributing a personal asset strengthens capital without inflating sales revenue.

questions.questionText: Compare FIFO (First In, First Out) and AVCO (Weighted Average Cost) inventory valuation methods during a period of rising prices (inflation), stating the effect on Gross Profit and Closing Inventory value. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**FIFO vs AVCO During Inflation — Valuation & Cost of Sales [2 marks]:** Under **FIFO (First In, First Out)** during a period of steadily rising purchase prices, the business assumes the **oldest, cheapest stock units** bought first are sold first (**charging lower historical costs into Cost of Sales**), leaving the **newest, most expensive units** sitting in the storeroom as **Higher Closing Inventory** [1 mark]. Under **AVCO (Weighted Average Cost)**, each new batch recalculates an updated average unit cost across all units in stock, smoothing out price spikes and giving an **intermediate Closing Inventory value** cleanly between older and newest prices [1 mark].

**Impact on Reported Gross Profit [2 marks]:** Because **Gross Profit = Sales - Cost of Goods Sold** and Cost of Goods Sold falls whenever Closing Inventory rises, **FIFO reports a HIGHER Gross Profit** during inflation than AVCO (which charges a higher weighted-average unit cost to Cost of Sales and reports a **slightly lower, more smoothed Gross Profit**). Conversely, if purchase prices fall steadily (deflation), those relative positions reverse cleanly.

**ZIMSEC Valuation Integrity & IAS 2 Prudence Rule:** Whatever cost formula (FIFO or AVCO) a firm adopts must be applied **consistently from year to year** (**Consistency Concept**) rather than swapped artificially to flatter profits, and total Closing Inventory must always be checked against **Net Realisable Value (lower of Cost and NRV)** so damaged or obsolete stock is never overstated.

questions.questionText: Explain why a business might show a healthy Net Profit of $20,000 on its Income Statement yet still suffer a bank overdraft (cash flow crisis). Give four specific reasons. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Reasons 1 & 2 — Credit Sales Lag & Non-Current Asset Purchases [2 marks]:** First, **Uncollected Credit Sales**: Income Statement Net Profit counts all **credit sales** invoiced during the year (**Accruals Concept**), even if huge sums remain unpaid inside **Trade Receivables**—high profit on paper produces zero bank cash until debtors settle [1 mark]. Second, **Capital Expenditure on Fixed Assets**: paying **$25,000 cash** to buy a delivery truck or new machinery drains the bank immediately, yet only the tiny **annual depreciation** (not the $25,000 purchase price!) enters the Income Statement [1 mark].

**Reasons 3 & 4 — Owner Drawings/Loan Repayments & Excess Inventory Tie-Up [2 marks]:** Third, **Heavy Drawings & Loan Principal Repayments**: owners drawing large personal salaries or repaying bank loan principal drain bank cash straight out without appearing anywhere as Income Statement expenses [1 mark]. Fourth, **Overstocking Inventory or Paying Suppliers Early**: tying up $15,000 cash buying huge extra warehouse stock sits as a **Current Asset (Closing Inventory)** rather than reducing Profit, sharply draining liquid cash reserves into an overdraft! [1 mark].

**Exam Synthesis — Profit Is Not Cash!** Mastering this distinction is vital in O-Level Accounting: **Profit** measures *accrued economic wealth earned* (**Revenue - Expenses**), whereas **Cash Flow / Bank Balance** tracks *physical money movement* (**Cash Inflows - Cash Outflows**). A rapidly expanding profitable firm often faces **overtrading**—going cash-broke while profitable—unless working capital (inventory, receivables, and credit terms) is tightly controlled.

questions.questionText:
From the following balances as at 31 December 2025, prepare a Statement of Financial Position extract showing Net Assets and Capital section:
Premises $45,000; Equipment $15,000 (Acc Dep $3,000); Inventory $6,200; Trade Receivables $4,800; Bank $1,500; Trade Payables $3,500; 5-Year Bank Loan $10,000; Opening Capital $48,000; Net Profit $11,500; Drawings $3,500. [7 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Non-Current Assets & Net Current Assets (Working Capital) [4 marks]:** Prepare the **Statement of Financial Position (Net Assets format)** cleanly in two vertical columns. Under **Non-Current Assets**, list **Premises ($45,000)** plus **Equipment Net Book Value ($15,000 Cost - $3,000 Acc. Dep. = $12,000)** giving **Total Non-Current Assets = $57,000** [2 marks]. Under **Current Assets**, sum **Inventory ($6,200) + Trade Receivables ($4,800) + Bank ($1,500) = $12,500**; less **Current Liabilities (Trade Payables $3,500)** yields **Net Current Assets (Working Capital) = $9,000** [2 marks].

**Non-Current Liabilities, Total Net Assets & Financed By Section [3 marks]:** Add Non-Current Assets (**$57,000**) plus Working Capital (**$9,000**) = **$66,000**, then deduct **Non-Current Liabilities (5-Year Bank Loan $10,000)** to obtain **Total Net Assets = $56,000**. Directly below under **Financed By (Capital Section)**: start with **Opening Capital ($48,000)**, add **Net Profit (+$11,500)** = **$59,500**, and deduct **Drawings (-$3,500)** to balance cleanly at **Closing Capital = $56,000**!

**Built-In Exam Proof & Formatting Tips:** Always verify that **Total Net Assets ($56,000) == Closing Capital ($56,000)** before moving to the next question—any mismatch warns immediately that a liability or contra-asset (like Accumulated Depreciation or Drawings) was added instead of subtracted. Remember to order **Current Assets** by increasing liquidity (**Inventory → Trade Receivables → Bank/Cash**) per standard ZIMSEC 4051 presentation.

questions.questionText:
Identify which accounting concept applies in each situation:
(a) Depreciation method should not be switched randomly from year to year.
(b) A $5 stapler is expensed immediately rather than depreciated over 5 years.
(c) Unpaid December telephone bill of $85 is included in 2025 expenses.
(d) Revenue is recognised when goods are delivered on credit, not when cash arrives later. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
**(a) Consistency Concept & (b) Materiality Concept [2 marks]:** **(a)** Keeping the chosen depreciation method steady from year to year exemplifies the **Consistency Concept**, ensuring profits across consecutive accounting years can be compared fairly without management cherry-picking methods to manipulate earnings [1 mark]. **(b)** Charging a trivial **$5 stapler** immediately to stationery expense instead of capitalising and depreciating it over 5 years exemplifies the **Materiality Concept**, because $5 is too insignificant to influence users’ financial decisions and tracking 5-year depreciation ($1/year) wastes time [1 mark].

**(c) Accruals (Matching) Concept & (d) Realisation Concept [2 marks]:** **(c)** Including December’s unpaid **$85 telephone bill** inside 2025 expenses upholds the **Accruals (Matching) Concept**, matching costs consumed in earning 2025 revenues strictly against 2025 income regardless of when cash is paid in January [1 mark]. **(d)** Recognising revenue once goods are delivered and legal ownership transfers on credit—rather than waiting for eventual debtor cash—upholds the **Realisation Concept** [1 mark].

**Distinguishing Overlapping Concepts in Paper 2:** Students frequently confuse **Consistency** with **Comparability** or **Accruals** with **Prudence**: link **Consistency** strictly to *unchanged accounting policies over time*, link **Materiality** to *size/significance of trivial items like calculators or staplers*, link **Accruals** to *unpaid/prepaid expenses & income matching the period*, and link **Realisation** to *exact timing when revenue is legitimately earned*!
